DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions?
  • It has been revealed that researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA.
  • Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

It has been revealed that researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists.

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An vital difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Sources indicate that why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

Recent findings suggest that to explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage.

According to recent reports, the results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," noted Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.".

According to recent reports, this finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

According to recent reports, the discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

New Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection.

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

Recent findings suggest that the team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," noted Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team strategy to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

In a recent development, A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins.".

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast.
  • As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.
  • Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know.

As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.

Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane.

It has been revealed that venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky. Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below.

Recent findings suggest that this is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification.

The bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky.

Spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope.

Check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease.

Sources indicate that want to get a closer look at the planets of the solar system and the stars beyond? Then be sure to check out our roundups of the best telescopes and smart telescopes for observing the night sky.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Best International Oscar race is the biggest ever — a record 104 international features are in contention, beating the previous high-water mark of 93 set in 2020 — and one of the most open in years.

There is no out-and-out favorite this season, although European cinema again looks strong, with Javier Calvo and Javier Abrosso’s Spanish entry La Bola Negra; Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord, in the running for Romania; and Pawel Pawlikowski’s Polish contender Fatherland all expected to make the short list, alongside Asian faves including South Korea’s Possible Love, from Lee Chang-dong; and Japan’s All of a Sudden from Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

Industry observers note that behind that top five is a long list of maybes, including French entry Minotaur from twice-nominated Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev; Lukas Dhont’s WWI drama Coward, Belgium’s entry; Austria’s Rose, which like Fatherland stars Sandra Huller; and Rehearsals for a Revolution, Pegah Ahangarani’s documentary on her family and their battles against the Iranian regime, which is the U.K. official Oscar submission.

In a recent development, one hundred films were submitted by countries or regions. Four qualified through a new method where movies that win top awards at leading festivals are accepted as long as they meet the language, creative input and theatrical-release requirements for the category. According to Academy rules, an international feature film is defined as a feature-length motion picture (more than 40 minutes) produced outside the United States with a predominantly (more than 50 percent) non-English dialogue track. New Zealand’s submission, Taratoa Stappard’s gothic horror tale Mārama, was dropped for falling short of the language requirement.

In a recent development, academy members from all branches who meet the minimum viewing requirements can participate in the preliminary round of voting for the shortlist, taking place between will take place Dec. 7-11. The shortlist of 15 international films will be announced on Dec. 15. Oscar nominations voting will take place Jan. 11-15, 2027, with the nominations announcement on Jan. 21.

The 99th Academy Awards will be held on March 14, 2027.

THR has exhaustively compiled the full list of international contenders, with trailers, reviews and talent interviews where available. Enjoy!

According to recent reports, roland Sejko’s documentary uses archival footage, newsreels and state-produced cinema to examine how Enver Hoxha’s communist regime used film as an instrument of propaganda. Tracing Albania’s isolation and political transformation over four decades, the film explores how the country’s official image was manufactured, controlled and disseminated by the state.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In 1993, a car crash leaves Ahmed amnesiac, so that not even his family feels familiar. His youngest son fears him and his bandaged face, while Ahmed feels uneasy about his neighbor. Yanis Koussim’s debut feature — the Arabic title means “exorcism” — reimagines the traumas of Algeria’s bloody “Black Decade” (1992–2002), a civil war between the government and Islamist rebel groups, as a horror film, blending memory, trauma and possession.

Teenage angst meets the supernatural in Laura Casabé’s coming-of-age horror film, set over a single lazy summer day in 2001, at the peak of Argentina’s great depression. Amid the backdrop of social unrest, adolescent desire turns deadly in this slow-burn rage thriller, which debuted at Sundance in 2025.

According to recent reports, tamara Stepanyan’s narrative feature debut follows Céline, a French woman who travels to Armenia to settle the affairs of her supposedly deceased husband, Arto. There she discovers that he concealed his past as a soldier and is regarded by some as a deserter. As she investigates his life, Céline encounters a country still haunted by successive wars and their unresolved consequences.

Read THR‘s interview with director Tamara Stepanyan here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

James J. Robinson’s debut feature is the country’s first-ever Tagalog-language submission for the Oscars. The meditative film focuses on an aging woman who questions her faith as the world crumbles around her. After a young construction worker dies under suspicious circumstances, an elderly nun whose life has been shaped by discipline, service and belief, gets drawn into a world of crime and corruption.

The trailer for First Light is below.

In a recent development, sandra Hüller is everywhere in this season’s awards conversation, but the German star gives her most transformative performance playing a 17th-Century woman passing as a male farmer in Markus Schleinzer’s period drama. Hüller won the Best Performance trophy in Berlin for the role, which was based on hundreds of similar recorded cases throughout history. Read THR’s review of Rose here.

Zaur Gasimli’s historical drama follows Azerbaijani philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev and his efforts to establish Baku’s first school for Muslim girls in 1901. Facing fierce opposition from religious conservatives, Taghiyev enlists the support of his young wife, Sona, in a campaign that becomes a test of his influence, diplomacy and determination to expand educational opportunities for women.

Mejbaur Rahman Sumon reimagines Adam and Eve in the monsoon-soaked Bengali countryside in this dark folk tale. A tenant farmer (Mostafizur Noor Imran) wants out of his arranged marriage to a woman (Nazifa Tushi) the villagers regard as insane. Promising her a trip to the circus, he rows her into the forest and slips away in the dark. Yet however far he takes her, the thud of a palm fruit beside their hut introduces her return. Sumon’s follow-up to Hawa, Bangladesh’s 2022 Oscar submission, premiered in Rotterdam’s Tiger Competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

Lukas Dhont’s queer World War I drama follows two Belgian soldiers, Pierre and Francis, who find an unexpected refuge from the brutality of the trenches in the world of theatre. Assigned to organize entertainment for their fellow troops, the men develop an increasingly intimate relationship as they put together a revue behind the front lines. Leads Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared the Best Actor prize at Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

This Turkish-language political drama from German Academy Award nominee İlker Çatak (The Teacher’s Lounge) qualified for Oscar submission by winning the Golden Bear for Best Film at the Berlinale. Özgü Namal and Tansu Biçer star as Derya and Aziz, a successful theatrical couple whose lives are upended after their latest production brings them into conflict with the authorities in Ankara. Dismissed from their jobs and forced to leave their home, they find their loss of professional standing and financial security puts their marriage under pressure, testing the convictions that once united them.

Read THR‘s interview with Çatak here and THR‘s review of Yellow Letters here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

The coming-of-age drama about tradition, ambition and choosing your own destiny follows a young woman in the Bolivian Andes who takes up the sacred ways of midwifery, but dreams of escaping to the city to become a singer. Directed by Álvaro Olmos Torrico, The Condor Daughter had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival.

A 60-something electrician has his very ordered life shattered by the sudden death of his wife. Left alone and forced to fend for himself in a strictly patriarchal society, he begins to recognize how much he took her devotion for granted. His attempts to reconnect with his estranged children are further complicated by his discovery that his son is living with another man.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Allan Deberton’s queer coming-of-age drama, which debuted in Berlin as part of the Generation Kplus section, follows a 12 year-old boy growing up in a small rural community trying balance his affection and desires with the fear of rejection from his father and surrounding community.

Check out a THR interview about the film here and the trailer below.

Nearly a decade after well-received 2017 feature Western, German director Valeska Grisebach returns with another deconstruction of a male-dominated genre. This slow-burning crime thriller, set in the Bulgarian borderlands, works as a low-key arthouse take on The Godfather, as archaeologist Veska (Yana Radeva) returns to the rural community she grew up in and reconnects with old friends, getting pulled back into criminal activity. Winner of the Jury Prize in Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

In a recent development, majid Majidi’s social drama, about Solan (Mohammad Rahimi), a poorly-paid temporary teacher in a remote, drought-stricken Iranian village was the stand out at this year’s Busan Film Festival, where it won the top prize, directly qualifying it for the Oscar race. When the death of the benefactor funding the school’s meal programme threatens to drive away the pupils, Solan takes matters into his own hands, turning to oil smuggling to keep the meals coming.

Check out the trailer for Midday Meal below.

Recent findings suggest that even the dead face eviction in Polen Ly’s elegiac ghost story about the cost of redevelopment in Cambodia. Thida (Savorn Serak) has watched over a movie house in Battambang since her death during the Khmer Rouge years. With the building marked for demolition, she must choose between wandering as a homeless spirit and risking the pain of another human life. She befriends Hai (Piseth Chhun), a young journalist who remembers going to the movies there as a boy. In the shuttered theater, the two watch a film together on his phone. Ly’s fiction feature debut premiered in Venice’s Biennale College Cinema program and won the Golden Hanoman, the top prize at Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival.

According to recent reports, nchini Sylvia-Bright is back in her second Cameroon Oscar submission after Ngang Romanus’ 2021 movie Hidden Dreams. In Mabanda, she plays Mojoko, a pregnant teenager who, after the death of her mother, is left alone with her abusive father, played by director Quintus, and faces rejection by her community. Shot in Cameroonian Pidgin English, it’s the eighth submission by the country for the Academy Awards.

Check out the first look trailer below.

This transatlantic drama from Montreal-based director Geneviève Dulude-De Celles bowed in Berlin, where it won the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay. It centers on an art expert, Mihail, who fled Bulgaria 30 years earlier and returns to authenticate the work of Nina, an 8-year-old Bulgarian artist and possible child prodigy, whose paintings have gone viral online. As Mikhail studies her work, he is forced to confront the ghosts of his past.

Check out the trailer for Nina Rosa below.

In a recent development, the period mystery, the director’s second feature, premiered at Cannes. The follow-up to Martelli’s General Augusto Pinochet-era political thriller Chile ‘76is set in 1992, after Pinochet’s regime ends and a 9-year old girl is staying in an Andean ski resort where she befriends a German teenager aiming to be a competitive skier, only to vanish without a trace.

Read the THR review and an interview with Martelli.

Check out the trailer for The Meltdown below.

Industry observers note that chinese comedy star Shen Teng plays a chef who takes a job in Bahata, a fictional stand-in for Baghdad, to pay off his family’s debts. In this war drama loosely inspired by the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Chinese restaurant where he works becomes both a refuge for local orphans and a bar for American soldiers. Director Wen Muye previously made a blockbuster out of the high cost of cancer drugs in China with 2018’s Dying to Survive. This latest social drama has grossed $358.4 million worldwide, making it by far the highest-grossing entry in this year’s international feature Oscar race.

In a recent development, A group of misfits converging at Babel, a legendary Colombian dive bar that doubles as purgatory, and where La Flaca — the city’s Grim Reaper — presides. Here, souls gamble years of their lives with her, daring to outwit Death herself. With his feature debut, which debuted at Sundance in 2025, director Gala del Sol has created a fantastical Colombian fever dream where life and death collides and the fate of people is left to chance.

Check out the official trailer below.

It has been revealed that with her debut feature, Costa Rica’s Kim Torres has created a rural chiller, combining story combining a coming-of-age drama with supernatural and thriller elements. The film follows 13-year-old Laura, who feels suffocated by her latest family, despite the lush forests and palm plantations that surround her. She soon discovers the supposed village paradise hides a shadowy secret that preys on the women living in it. Torres’ drama world premiered at San Sebastian’s New Directors sidebar in 2025.

Sources indicate that director Hana Jusic took inspiration from Wuthering Heights and gothic horror in this period drama, set in rural Croatia, circa 1910, to tell a surprisingly modern tale of female liberation. Teresa, a Chilean woman dressed all in black like an avenging angel, arrives in an isolated, and deeply religious community of Croatian shepherds in the early 20th century, claiming to be the widow of a local man who emigrated to South America.

Her arrival unsettles the tightly ordered society, challenging its traditional relationships and expectations. Unable to speak the language, she becomes a blank canvas for hopes and fears, particularly of the women in the community.

You can read a director interview here and watch the THR Presents interview with Hana Jusic here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Carlos Larrazabal’s debut feature explores the pull of home and the longing to leave. It follows Elvis, who returns to Havana after spending a decade in prison for murdering his abusive stepfather. As he reconnects with childhood sweetheart and falls back into life in the city’s criminal underworld, Elvis must decide whether to stay in the world he knows or escape Havana for a upcoming life elsewhere.

Cyprus’ first-ever international Oscar contender is also the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis, who played the son in Yorgos Lanthimos’ Dogtooth, star as an 11-year-old and her absent, petty criminal father who returns home after a family death. The film won The World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award at Sundance.

Check out the THR’s Presents interview with Myrsini Aristidou here and read an earlier interview with her here.

Prague-based filmmaker Pepa Lubojacki scoured through family photos and diary snapshots for this intimate, heart-rending look at her family’s struggles with alcoholism, addiction and homelessness. The film premiered in Berlin, where it won the best documentary honor as well as the independent Caligari award.

Industry observers note that this historical thriller from directors Yohane Dean Lengol and Hamed Mobasser is set in 1959, in the final months of Belgian colonial rule, in Club Rumba Royale, a popular nightclub where white Europeans and Congolese citizens rub shoulders as dance mixes with debates of independence. Featuring African rumba star Fally Ipupa, the feature is the first submission by DR Congo since 1997 and only the second overall.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

It has been revealed that may el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion-winning Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Volpi Cup winner Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret.

It has been revealed that the Danish filmmaker deftly scrutinizes post-war patriotism and the era’s chastisement of women and their sex lives. “There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true,” el-Toukhy told THR ahead of Venice. “But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me.”.

Read THR‘s interview with May el-Toukhy here.

Check out a clip from Woman Unknown below.

Recent findings suggest that the second feature film from director Andrés Farías centers on Sonia (Mercedes Morales), a widow who trades her family home for a cramped apartment and finds unexpected intimacy with Aimé, a working-class Haitian man, defying her family and the racial tensions between Dominicans and Haitians. The drama played Havana, Miami and Chicago and won best film, director and actress at the 2026 Dominican Film Festival in New York.

Recent findings suggest that director Cristina Barragán, who represented Ecuador in 2016 with Alba, continues her exploration of childhood wounds in this drama starring Simone Bucio as Azucena, a woman in her 30s who approaches Julio, a teenager in a group home, played by first-time actor Francis Eddú Llumiquinga. As they spend time together, an uneasy closeness grows, changing the personal bond in ways two outsiders from different worlds, but with a shared experience of trauma, The film won the best screenplay award in the Orizzonti section at the Venice Film Festival.

It has been revealed that the Egyptian-Austrian filmmaker Abu Bakr Shawky is back in the international Oscar race after his 2018 feature Yomeddine, also submitted for Egypt. The Stories, loosely inspired by his own parents’ relationship, follows aspiring Cairo pianist Ahmed and his long-distance romance with Austrian pen pal Liz, from the 1960s through the 1980s. Starring Amir El-Masry (The Crown) and Valerie Pachner (Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore).

Read what the director mentioned about The Stories here and then check out the trailer below.

Arturo López Rodas wrote, directed and produced this debut feature, a 60-minute drama in which three old friends reunite for a funeral after decades apart, musing on life, loss and time. It won best screenplay at the Ícaro Awards and best international feature at the Cobb International Film Festival. Vértices represents El Salvador’s first entry into Oscar’s best international feature competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

Sources indicate that in his feature film debut, director German Golub charts the real-life story of Erika Salumäe, a track cyclist who overcomes personal and professional hardship — and the pressure of the dwindling Soviet regime — to become a two-time Olympic gold medallist in 1988 and 1992. From troubled young woman to national hero, Salumäe’s tenacity makes this biographical sports drama a story of inspiration and grit, with Estonian actress Karolin Jürise in the titular role.

Check out the trailer for Our Erika below.

Sources indicate that finnish filmmaker Markus Lehmusruusu (2019’s Ricky Rapper and the Strong Man) turns to science fiction in his sophomore feature. In a future, sterile world without nature or animals, Pasi (Miro Lopperi) is a lonely and compassionate designer of synthetic pets.

Sources indicate that when by chance he stumbles upon the last surviving squirrel, he decides to defy the very strict regulations of interaction with what little nature is left in the world and help the squirrel back into its natural habitat. Lehmusruusu tackles the intersection of humanity’s instinctive need to both survive and provide in this Fantastic Fest debut (which used real, trained squirrels over animatronics or VFX).

Check out the trailer for The Squirrel below.

The first feature film from exiled Russian dissident director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan) in nearly a decade is a taut psychological thriller set in Russia shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Loosely inspired by Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969) it follows a wealthy businessman caught between government demands that he recruit employees to send as cannon fodder in the war effort, and his growing suspicions that his wife is having an affair. As pressure mounts on both fronts, his carefully controlled domestic and professional life begins to unravel. Like the Russian state, he goes to extremes of violence to maintain the appearance of power and control.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Andrey Zvyagintsev here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In a recent development, levan Koguashvili’s dramedy is set in a Georgian village struggling to recover from the economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union. At its center is Zuriko, a widowed hazelnut farmer trying to secure a fair price for his harvest while his debts mount. With the help of his friend Gela, he also embarks on a search for a fresh partner, despite the objections of his formidable former mother-in-law.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

In a recent development, birgit Minichmayr plays Ella, a mother struggling to process the death of her daughter Jessie, in Sandra Wollner’s drama about grief and the complicated bonds left behind. Ella begins spending time with Lux, Jessie’s boyfriend, who was with her on the night she died. As the two grow closer, their relationship becomes increasingly entangled with memories of the young woman. An impulsive family holiday to Tenerife becomes an increasingly surreal attempt to escape grief and reconnect with the past.

A favorite in Cannes, where it won Best Film of the Un Certain Regard section, Everytime has been nominated for Best Film and Wollner for Best Screenplay at the 2027 European Film Awards.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Sandra Wollner here.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

In a recent development, yannis Economides crafts a modern Greek tragedy out of the story of a businessman who devises what appears to be a foolproof scheme to save his family home from falling into the hands of a loan shark. But his plan sets a series of increasingly unpredictable events in motion, threatening to destroy the very life he is trying to preserve.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Sources indicate that guatemalan auteur Jayro Bustamante returns with an action-tinged drama inspired by the true story of Guatemala’s 2018 Volcán de Fuego tragedy. María Mercedes Coroy plays a volcanologist who tries to warn and evacuate Indigenous communities as a new volcano forms amid corruption and economic interests. This is Bustamante’s fourth Oscar submission, after 2015’s Ixcanul, 2019’s La Llorona (shortlisted) and Rita from 2024.

Check out the official trailer (no subtitles) below.

Snow falls on Hong Kong in Juno Mak’s underworld epic, in which a hospital bombing kills a pharmaceutical magnate and leaves his younger son with an unusual ambition for a family drug empire — to shut it all down. A long-in-the-making saga starring Asian industry heavyweights Takeshi Kaneshiro, Tony Leung Ka-fai and Louis Koo, the film premiered in Cannes and won eight Hong Kong Film Awards, including one for its score by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto.

Tony Leung Chiu-wai, Léa Seydoux and fast-rising German star Luna Wedler feature in this century-spanning contemplative drama from Hungarian auteur Ildikó Enyedi (On Body and Soul, The Story of My Wife). Set in three different eras — 1908, 1972, and 2020 — it follows three very different people, a pioneering female student, a lovesick young man and a Hong Kong neuroscientist who share a connection to an ancient ginkgo tree growing int the botanical garden of a German university town. Enigmatic but never self-serious, Silent Friend leavens its massive ideas and visual poetry with a healthy dose of deadpan humor.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with Silent Friend star Luna Wedler here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Sources indicate that yrsa Roca Fannberg turns her camera on the residents and caregivers of a Reykjavík nursing home in this observational documentary about ageing and the final stages of life. Everyday activities, from dancing and exercise classes to painting nails and sharing quiet moments, become the focus of an intimate portrait of a community negotiating the realities of old age. Rather than concentrating on decline, the film finds moments of companionship, humour and pleasure in the routines of institutional life.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Set in a remote Naga village near the Myanmar border in the early 1960s, Theja Rio’s debut feature follows Anghba, the community’s last surviving chief. With most of the villagers having left, he remains with his ailing wife and speech-impaired son, struggling to preserve the traditions of his ancestors. The arrival of an American missionary introduces Christianity and new social customs, deepening the generational divide between father and son. The film won the Platform Award at Toronto, qualifying it for the Oscar race.

Read THR India‘s review of Angh here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

In Santosh Davakhar’s Marathi-language folk thriller, a young bride in rural Maharashtra plots her groom’s murder during the traditional ceremony meant to bless their marriage. As the village gathers for the gondhal, an all-night ritual of devotional song and dance, Suman (Ishita Deshmukh) recruits the groom’s cousin, a former suitor, to do the killing so she can run away with one of the performers. The film won Davakhar the Silver Peacock for best director at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

It has been revealed that director Kamila Andini (Yuni) drew on the testimony of sexual assault survivors for this magical realist drama about the patriarchal structures of a Javanese mountain village. Putri Marino plays Pertiwi, who spent 20 years in prison for killing an accomplice to her rape at 16. She comes home to find the men who sent her away now running the village. When she meets a deaf teenage girl whose ordeal echoes her own, Pertiwi rallies her fellow outcasts to bring the abuse to light. The film premiered in Toronto, and Marino shared the best performance prize at the Singapore International Film Festival.

Babak Khajehpasha’s anti-war drama captures the lives and dreams of children and adults in Gaza against the backdrop of an ongoing conflict and crisis with Israel. The film cast child actors of Arab, Iranian, Syrian, and Lebanese backgrounds alongside Iranian performers.

It has been revealed that rather than depict violent battlefield scenes, the Iranian filmmaker focused on the all-too human impact of war on children as they learn fear, death and waiting are part of their everyday lives. The film also strikes a note of hope that love and life can be kept alive during horrific war and strife.

The Iraqi feature, which premiered out of competition in Venice, follows a female Kurdish sniper, Vyan, who returns to Mosul to try and rescue her younger sister. She has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she goes all out to rescue her. Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, found inspiration for the film from an encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that A robbery at a rural credit union ends in tragedy, but Damian McCann’s Irish-language thriller works backwards to reveal how three women became involved in the botched operation. Carrie Crowley, Bríd Brennan and Eva-Jane Gaffney star as the unlikely accomplices at the center of a story involving desperation, criminal ambition and a woman on the verge of a breakdown.

Check out the trailer for Aontas below.

The Israeli film, set in 1987, centers on a 12-year-old boy, Boaz, who while preparing for his bar mitzvah is shocked to witness his father having sex in a swimming pool locker room. The boy’s family life is upturned just as the AIDS epidemic takes hold. But a decade later, the father and his older son attempt to reconcile and accept one another.

Rosenthal’s film, titled Independence in Hebrew, premiered at Sundance and won the top best picture award at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s Academy Awards entry.

Check out the trailer for Tell Me Everything below.

Recent findings suggest that paolo Strippoli’s psychological thriller is one of the rare genre romps among the mostly serious dramas in this season’s international Oscar race. Jasmine Trinca plays a housewife so desperate to have the perfect family she makes a faustian bargain with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s chain-smoking stranger, triggering a series of events that, over the course of decades, will bring her family crashing down. New Line has already snatched up English remake rights to this twisty crowd pleaser.

Read THR‘s review of The Spiral here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Sources indicate that ryusuke Hamaguchi’s first French feature begins as a workplace drama set in a nursing home outside Paris and blossoms into a love story about two women falling for each other’s minds. Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira) asks her overstretched nurses to employ a more humane system of care for residents living with dementia. Watching a play about life in a psychiatric institution, she recognizes her own convictions in the work of its Japanese director, Mari (Tao Okamoto), who is dying of cancer.

Recent findings suggest that the women connect and talk deep into the night, slipping between French and Japanese, and there’s such pleasure in their exchanges that even Mari’s impromptu whiteboard lecture on capitalism feels like a moment of deep emotional connection. Efira and Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes. After winning the international feature Oscar for Drive My Car in 2022, Hamaguchi is again considered a frontrunner this season.

Read THR‘s interview with All of a Sudden co-stars Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira here.

The film’s official trailer is below.

Sink is a drama about a mother navigating her son’s mental health crisis — still a taboo subject in Jordan — by denying her son’s struggles and opting instead to see his emotional withdrawal and disruptive behavior at school as teenage rebellion. So the mother follows her son about with devotion, hoping her guidance at attention will prove a cure. Duraie’s debut feature, following her acclaimed short films Horizon and Give up the Ghost, had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival, nd.

Abel is a shepherd living on a collective farm in Kazakhstan whose life in thrown into turmoil in the 1990s when, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, collective farms were dismantled and divided up among corrupt leaders. The aging Abel has a choice: play along for a piece of the action or stand up for what he believes is right.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Writer-director Vincho Nchogu serves up a mix of comedy and drama in her feature debut. Sarah Karei plays Star, an orphaned and unmarried 38-year-old woman in a rural village who risks losing her home unless she can prove her family lineage and claim her land deed. Along the way she has to deal with hostile neighbors, shady organizations and the promise of potential romance. Winner of the audience award at Tribeca and the Best First Feature prize at the BFI London Film Festival.

Blerta Basholli takes a coming-of-age story into the increasingly volatile atmosphere of late-1990s Kosovo. Thirteen-year-old Dua is navigating the usual uncertainties of adolescence when an incident turns her into a target within her community. Her friendship with the outspoken Maki offers a latest perspective on the world around her, even as the escalating conflict threatens to overwhelm their lives.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Bekzat Pirmatov blends psychological horror, folklore and family drama in this supernatural tale about a grieving woman plagued by a recurring nightmare in which an unseen presence appears to strangle her in her sleep. Seeking an explanation, she turns to a traditional healer who discovers ominous markings on the bodies of pregnant women. Their investigation leads to the ancient Kyrgyz legend of Albarsty, a malevolent female spirit associated with pregnancy and childbirth.

In a recent development, A biographical sports drama from Viesturs Kairišs, who co-wrote Ulya with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, Livia Ulman, and Andris Feldmanis. The Cannes-premiering, black-and-white feature is set in rural Soviet Latvia in 1964, where Uļjana “Ulya” Semjonova’s (Kārlis Arnolds Avots) attracts the attention of basketball scouts due to her exceptional height and strength. She’s pulled from farm life into elite sport in this mise-en-scène-embracing portrait of a Latvian legend.

Read THR‘s interview with director Viesturs Kairišs here.

Check out THR‘s portrait of Ulya star and co-screenwriter Karlis Arnolds Avots here.

It has been revealed that lebanon’s Oscar hopeful is a heist thriller about two sisters who concoct an elaborate initiative to break into a bank to steal their own money — the cash frozen by the government during the 2019 Lebanese liquidity crisis — to fund a life-saving operation. Director Rami Kodeih co-wrote the film with his wife Nora Mariana inspired by their own experience at the time, when Mariana needed surgery and their savings were inaccessible. George Clooney and Grant Heslov are executive producers for Smokehouse Pictures.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out a clip from the film below.

How to Divorce During the War is exactly as it sounds — a high-flying executive Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite) chooses the worst possible moment to inform her struggling filmmaker husband Vytas (Marius Repsys) she wants to split up: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Vilnius-set, soul-searching drama won director Andrius Blaževičius a directing award upon its Sundance premiere.

According to recent reports, this jump scare-heavy psychological horror from debut feature filmmaker Cyrus Neshvad (already an Oscar nominee for 2023 short The Red Suitcase) follows a family in dire straits. With their young son not having much time left, Anne and Greg are ready to sacrifice everything to give him one last chance at salvation. But after crossing an unforgivable moral line, they find themselves trapped in a nightmare where every choice comes with an ever-higher price. Child earned its world premiere at the 2026 Raindance Film Festival.

Check out the official trailer below.

Woo Ming Jin drew on his own childhood as a twin for this coming-of-age drama about two teenage brothers in a Malaysian coastal town. At 15, Ali is the only person who understands his twin brother Amir’s way of communicating. When their father remarries, he packs the boys off to work in a salted-fish factory. But it’s their shared crush on their new English teacher (Indonesian star Dian Sastrowardoyo) that turns the brothers into rivals. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival.

In a recent development, żejtune is a visually rich Maltese-language drama from the Latest York-based Alex Camilleri, led by Michela Farrugia as Mar. When her estranged mother passes away, Mar sees her way out of Malta by selling off her inheritance: three pieces of farmland in the countryside. On her journey to claim her land, she meets Nenu, a spirited 80-year-old singer (Nenu Borg) whose vibrant folk music pulls her into the colourful traditions of the island she’s been so eager to escape. The movie hit the festival circuit with appearances at Gothenburg and Tribeca.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

David Pablos’ drama follows Veneno (Víctor Prieto), a rebellious young drifter who sleeps with truckers at roadside diners. He persuades one of his hook ups, Muñeco (Osvaldo Sánchez) to take him deep into the hyper-masculine world of long-haul trucking. The road movie, produced by Diego Luna, won best film in Venice’s Orizzonti section as well as the Queer Lion.

Read THR‘s review of On The Road here.

Mongolia’s struggle to end more than two centuries of Qing rule takes the shape of an espionage thriller in Tamir Bat-Ulzii’s sweeping historical epic. The actor-director casts himself as Namnansuren, the statesman who joined forces with the Buddhist leader Bogd Khan in 1911. The conspirators seek help from Russia while building a network of spies at home. Made to mark the 115th anniversary of Mongolia’s declaration of independence, the film became one of the country’s biggest local hits this year.

Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić drummed up excitement in Sundance with To Hold a Mountain, a documentary shot in the Montenegrin highlands where a shepherdess and her adopted daughter are haunted by the violent death of her mother and must defend their mountain against its transformation into a NATO military training ground. This tender, windswept feature picked up the Grand Jury Prize in Sundance and the Heart of Sarajevo in the fest’s documentary competition section.

Laïla Marrakchi offers a new spin on the familiarly-bleak tale of migrant labor and exploitation in this social realist drama, inspired by real-life cases of Moroccan women who travel to Spain to work as seasonal fruit-pickers. Her protagonist Hasna (Nisrin Erradi) is a flawed, even unlikable character doing what she needs to survive in a world where oppression and coercion are the norm. Strawberries premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section.

Read THR‘s interview with Laila Marrakchi here.

It has been revealed that abinash Bikram Shah’s debut, the first Nepali feature to screen in Cannes’ Official Selection, won the jury prize in Un Certain Regard. The richly-realized missing-person thriller follows Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama), the matriarch of a Kinnar community of trans women in rural Nepal. Pirati dreams of slipping away with the man she loves. But when one of the young women she calls her daughters vanishes on a night patrol to keep wild elephants out of the village, she puts those plans on hold to search for her.

Read THR India’s interview with Abinash Bikram Shah here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Sources indicate that afghan-Dutch filmmaker Dawood Hilmandi turns the camera on his own family history in this intimate documentary about war, exile and an attempt at reconciliation with his estranged father. Having fled Afghanistan and later Iran, Hilmandi has made a home in Amsterdam, but a personal loss prompts him to return to his father, an aging, authoritarian former mujahideen fighter. Together they revisit the past, travelling between Iran and Afghanistan in an effort to overcome decades of silence, inherited trauma and estrangement. The film won three prizes at IDFA, including Best First Feature and the FIPRESCI international critics award.

Check out the trailer for Paikar below.

Sisters Ade and Titi lead very different lives under the shadow of their late father. The older Ade (Bimbo Akintola) is a devout Christian and the family’s sole breadwinner, while Titi (Tosin Adeyemi) is an aspiring singer full of independent spirit. When their ailing mother comes to live with them, old resentments resurface, forcing both sisters to confront grief and the fragile bonds that hold a family together.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Kosara Mitić’s debut feature 17, co-written by Ognjen Sviličić, arrived at this year’s Berlinale with a fierce exploration of sexual trauma and female solidarity. The movie follows seventeen-year-old Sara (Eva Kostic), who’s hiding a secret during a school trip. When the trip spirals out of control and she witnesses her friend Lina being sexually assaulted, the two girls try to break the cycle of casual violence and seal an everlasting bond between them in the process.

Read THR‘s interview with 17 director Kosara Mitić here.

#127825. A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today.
  • The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes.
  • In a recent development, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve vital biological functions.

In a recent development, in a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Sources indicate that jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation.

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

Recent findings suggest that this research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject.".

Sources indicate that gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," remarked Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.".

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island.

According to recent reports, jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

Recent findings suggest that today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

Has AI just cracked Internet encryption? Rumoured ‘bombshell’ stuns scientists

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty.
  • In a recent development, artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans.
  • Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty.

In a recent development, artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans. Now, a threat is emerging that is on a whole other scale.

Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs.

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote yesterday on his blog. The details are still hazy, added Aaronson, who is at the University of Texas at Austin. “Until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”.

The algorithms are rumoured to target the information-scrambling system known as RSA, which relies on the mathematics of prime numbers, as well as more-advanced technologies.

While the rumours could not be confirmed, other breakthroughs announced by the AI companies this week make researchers cautiously optimistic that the mathematics of encryption could eventually come to help.

Nature examines the threat, and what can be done about it.

Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from banking apps to Internet browsers. It relies on mathematical problems that are considered practically impossible for computers to solve within a reasonable amount of time.

In a recent development, an algorithm that could solve these problems in polynomial time would change that. It means the time needed to solve a problem would increase relatively slowly as the problem gets larger. For example, a password of length n could be broken in a number of steps proportional to the square or cube of its size (n² or n³).

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers.

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers.

Recent findings suggest that theoretical computer scientists tend to think of P problems as relatively easy to solve, especially compared with problems that require exponential time, where the number of steps might grow as 2n, for example. As n gets larger — or a password gets longer — the time required by an exponential algorithm quickly exceeds that of any polynomial one.

In practical terms, an algorithm that could break public-key cryptography in polynomial time could undermine much of the security on which the Internet relies.

It depends on which encryption systems they could crack, and how efficiently they could do so.

One of the most ubiquitous techniques for establishing public keys is to multiply two large prime numbers. This technique, called RSA, was long believed to be secure because ‘cracking the code’ requires factoring that product back into the original primes, a much slower process (at least, without a powerful quantum computer, which does not yet exist). One of the rumours now circulating is that the AI labs have found an algorithm that can do this.

Sources indicate that but even though a polynomial-time algorithm could be very powerful on paper, it could still be impossible to use except for the shortest passwords. An algorithm requiring n10000steps, for example, be very impractical to apply.

However, proving that a problem is in ‘P’, even if the polynomial-time solution is practically useless, has usually been followed by improvements that have eventually led to efficient solutions. “The matter is that the idea that [the problem] was hard — because of needing exponential time — is dead,” Aaronson tells Nature.

It has been revealed that not necessarily. This type of worst-case scenario hinges on a long-standing open question known as ‘P = NP’: could every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time? If so, problems that underpin essentially all public-key cryptography could become much easier to crack.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security.

But most researchers think that this is unlikely. In fact, some recent AI-aided results have made them cautiously optimistic. Earlier this week, both Anthropic and OpenAI unveiled results in theoretical computer science that suggest that many similar problems could be hard to solve. Before the recent explosion in AI-aided maths, each of those advances would have been hailed as the computer-science breakthrough of the decade, Aaronson says.

Industry observers note that ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, agrees. “I am definitely blown away by the latest developments.” One especially interesting result, he says, shows that for a ubiquitous type of computation called matrix multiplication, the exponent in a polynomial-time algorithm cannot be too small. “Underneath the hood, it seems to provide a brand-latest framework for proving limitations on efficient computation,” says Williams.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration mentioned Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to concern a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Sources indicate that tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy remarked Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

According to recent reports, duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and stated it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing upcoming details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • In a recent development, newly introduced research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing upcoming details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide important clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

In a recent development, newly introduced research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Important Clues.

It has been revealed that dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

In a recent development, "The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan remarked.

It has been revealed that "Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

"By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

To investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

Sources indicate that these findings offer a upcoming perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

Industry observers note that the implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

"The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan said.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a new era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

Sources indicate that the return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.
